transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi. Thanks for seeing me. I, uh, I guess I'm here because things have just gotten really out of hand lately. You see, I'm not working right now, so I'm around the house all day, but it's really the nights that are the main problem for me. Most nights, after my wife goes up to bed—she usually heads up around 10 or 10:30 because she likes to read a bit before sleep, and the house just gets so incredibly quiet—I almost always end up wandering into the kitchen. 

And it's not like I'm just grabbing a normal midnight snack, you know, like a piece of fruit or a cracker. I start eating, and I eat way, way past what anyone would ever consider a normal plate of food. Like, if we had a family get-together or a party recently, I'll pull out all the heavy stuff. The cold fried chicken, the big Tupperware containers of mac and cheese, the sweet potatoes, those little dinner rolls... really just whatever event leftovers are sitting in there. I'll tell myself I'm just having a taste, but then I'm having another, and another, and I just keep going and going until an entire catering tray is completely scraped clean, or literally half the food in the fridge is just... gone. I don't even know how I fit it all in sometimes, but I'll just stand there in the kitchen and completely clear out whatever we have stored away. It's just happening almost every single night now, and I just... I don't know, it's a lot.
How do you feel after one of these late-night eating episodes?

Well, honestly... it's just awful. I mean, physically I feel terrible, obviously, because I've just stuffed myself to the brim, but mentally... mentally it's just this crushing weight. Like, immediately after I finish that last bite, or when I look down and see the empty containers stacked up on the counter, it just hits me all at once. I feel so incredibly sick with myself. 

And it's not just a passing thought, you know? It's this deep, heavy feeling in my gut. I think about how people see me—my wife, my friends, the people I used to work with. They all think of me as this organized, capable, strong guy who has everything under control. But then there I am, standing in the kitchen in the middle of the night, surrounded by crumbs and empty Tupperware, and I just feel so ashamed. I feel guilty for wasting the food, guilty for hiding it from my wife, and just absolutely disgusted with myself that I let it happen again. I always tell myself, "Okay, tonight's the night I stop, tonight I'll just have a glass of water and go back to bed," but then I don't. And when it's over, the disgust is just... it's overwhelming. I just sit there in the quiet and think, "What is wrong with me?" It's like I'm two different people, the guy during the day and this... this person at night who just completely loses control.
Do you ever make yourself vomit or use laxatives after one of these eating episodes?

No, no, I've never done anything like that. I know some people do, you know, they throw up or take pills to try and undo it, but I just... I don't. I just sit there with it. I mean, the thought of making myself sick, it just doesn't even cross my mind, really. I just feel so heavy, physically and emotionally, and I just kind of drag myself back up the stairs to bed. 

It's actually kind of funny, in a dark way, because I'll lie there in the dark, and my stomach will be in absolute knots, just stretching and aching from all that food—like that time last week after my niece's birthday party, I ate maybe three-quarters of a sheet cake all by myself, plus I don't even know how many leftover hot dogs, and I was just lying there sweating, feeling like I was going to burst. But I just ride it out. I just lie there and let the guilt and the stomachache just wash over me until I finally manage to pass out. I don't try to get rid of it. I just... I just carry it. Literally and figuratively, I guess. I just wake up the next morning feeling bloated and gross and exhausted, and the cycle just starts all over again. But no, no throwing up, no laxatives, nothing like that. I just suffer through the aftermath.
How often do you have these late-night eating episodes where you consume a large amount of food?

Well, it's... it's a lot. I mean, if I really sit back and think about it, it's been going on for months now. Honestly, for months, I can't think of a single week where it didn't happen at least once. Not one week. And, you know, it's rarely just once. Most weeks, it's several nights. 

Like I was saying before, it's always after my wife goes up to bed. She's got her routine, right? Brushes her teeth, washes her face, gets into bed with her book—lately she's been reading these thick historical biographies, so she's up there for a good while before she actually turns the light out. And I'll just be downstairs. I might be watching TV, or scrolling on my phone, or just sitting there in the living room, and the house gets so quiet you can hear the hum of the refrigerator. And that's when it starts. 

So, yeah, it's several nights a week. Sometimes it's three nights, sometimes it's four or five. Last week, I think it was Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. It's just this constant, looming thing. I'll wake up in the morning and tell myself, "Okay, tonight is going to be different. Tonight I'm just going to watch the game, drink some water, and go to sleep." But then 10:30 rolls around, she heads upstairs, and it's like a switch flips in my brain. The pull to go into the kitchen is just so strong. I'll walk in there, open the fridge, and it's like I'm on autopilot. Before I know it, it's happened again. So, to answer your question, it's almost constantly happening. Multiple times a week, every single week, for months on end now. I just can't seem to break the cycle.
Do you notice any specific emotions or thoughts that trigger your desire to eat at night?

Well, that's... that's the thing, I'm not really sure. I mean, I've tried to sit down and figure it out, you know? Like, really analyze what's going through my head right before I start eating. I'll sit there in the living room, and I'll try to pinpoint, "Okay, am I sad right now? Am I stressed about money? Am I worried about finding a job?" Because, you know, being out of work right now, there's a lot of stress. I left my last job back in October, and it's been this constant weight. So you'd think it would be that, right? You'd think I'd be sitting there worrying about the mortgage or whatever, and then I'd go eat to feel better.

But honestly... I don't really notice anything specific like that. It's not like I'm sitting there crying or having a panic attack and then I run to the fridge. It's more just... this emptiness, almost? Or maybe just boredom? I don't know if boredom is the right word, because it feels more intense than just being bored. But it's just this quiet. The house is so quiet. My wife is upstairs, the dog is asleep on his bed in the corner, the TV is just kind of murmuring in the background, and there's just... nothing happening. And it's almost like the quiet itself is the trigger. 

I don't have this big, flashing thought of, "I am so upset, I need a sandwich." It's more like a physical pull. I just start thinking about the kitchen. I'll picture the leftover lasagna in the Tupperware with the red lid, or the bag of chips sitting on the second shelf of the pantry, right next to the peanut butter. And once that image is in my head, it's just... it's all I can think about. But as for an actual emotion or a specific worry? I really haven't noticed one. It just feels like an automatic response to the house being empty and quiet, like my brain just says, "Well, it's time to go eat now," and I just get up and do it without really feeling anything at all until the guilt hits me afterward.
Do you feel like you have control over what you're eating or the amount you're eating during these late-night episodes?

No. No, none at all. That's the scariest part, honestly. It's like... it's like I'm not even driving the car anymore. I'm just in the passenger seat watching it crash. 

I'll be standing there in the kitchen, right? The refrigerator door is open, the little light is on, casting that weird glow on the linoleum, and I'll tell myself, "Okay, George, just one slice of cheese. Just one slice and we go back to the couch." But then I take that first bite, and it's like... it's like the decision has already been made for me. The cheese is gone, and then I'm reaching for the leftover Chinese food in the back, the one in the white carton with the metal handle, and I'm not even heating it up. I'm just eating cold lo mein straight out of the box with a fork I grabbed from the drying rack. 

And the whole time, my brain is screaming at me. I'm literally standing there, chewing, and I'm telling myself, "George, stop now. Put the fork down. Close the carton. Put it back." I'm having this entire internal argument with myself, begging myself to stop, but my hands... my hands just keep moving. They keep fixing another plate, or opening another container, or tearing open a bag of pretzels. It's like my body has been hijacked. I'll finish the Chinese food, and then I'll move on to a sleeve of crackers, and then maybe a bowl of cereal, pouring the milk in so carefully so it doesn't splash and make a sound that might wake my wife up. 

I know I'm full. I know I shouldn't be eating it. I know how awful I'm going to feel in twenty minutes, but I just can't physically make myself stop until I'm so stuffed I can barely breathe. It's completely out of my hands once I start. Completely.
Do you usually feel hungry before you start eating at night?

No, not really. Actually, a lot of the time I'm not hungry at all. I mean, it's crazy when you think about it, because you'd assume someone eating that much food must be starving, right? Like they haven't eaten a single thing all day. But for me, it's... it's the exact opposite. 

I might have just eaten a really big, filling dinner with my wife. Like, just a few days ago, she made this huge shepherd's pie—she uses ground turkey instead of beef to be a little healthier, and puts this nice thick crust of mashed potatoes on top with a little paprika—and we sat down at the dining table, ate a proper meal together, had a side salad with it, the whole nine yards. I was full. I was completely, totally satisfied. My stomach was physically full. 

But then, you know, a couple of hours pass, she goes upstairs to read her book like I mentioned before, and even though my stomach is literally still digesting dinner, even though there is absolutely zero physical hunger... I still go back into the kitchen. I'll just start picking at the leftovers. I'll take a fork and just kind of shave off a little piece of the pie from the pan on the stove while I'm supposed to be putting it away in the Tupperware. And then maybe I take a little more. And then I'm pulling out other things from the fridge, maybe some cheese, maybe some bread, and before I know it, it turns into another full-on spread right there on the counter. 

It's not about hunger at all. My stomach isn't growling. I'm not feeling weak or lightheaded or anything that tells your body it's time to eat. I just start picking at things, and then it snowballs into this massive amount of food, even though I'm already completely full from the dinner I just had. So, yeah, hunger really doesn't have anything to do with it. It's just... it's something else entirely, and I don't really know how to stop it once I start picking.
Have you noticed any significant weight gain since these late-night eating episodes started?

You know, that's the one thing that really confuses me about all of this. Because you would think, with the sheer volume of food I'm putting away—like I said, the whole cartons of Chinese food, the sleeves of crackers, the blocks of cheese—you'd think I'd be putting on ten pounds a week, right? I mean, it's just basic math, calories in versus calories out. But... no. I actually haven't noticed any major weight gain at all. 

It's the strangest thing. I still step on the scale in our master bathroom—it's this older digital one we got at Target years ago, the kind where you have to tap it with your foot first to wake it up before you actually step on it—and the number really hasn't budged much. Maybe a pound or two fluctuating, which I think is pretty normal for anyone, depending on water weight or whatever. And my clothes still fit exactly the same. I have these khaki pants I used to wear to the office before I left in October, and I put them on the other day just to see. Just out of pure paranoia, really, because I was sitting there thinking, "George, there's no way you aren't ballooning up with all this garbage you're eating at 2 AM." But they buttoned up just fine. No pinching at the waist, no having to suck in my gut to get the zipper up. 

It's almost like my body is just... I don't know, ignoring it? Or maybe my metabolism is just naturally fast enough to handle it right now? I really don't know how it's physically possible, but it almost makes me feel worse in a way. Because it's like this invisible secret. If I were gaining a ton of weight, at least there would be a physical sign of what I'm doing to myself, right? Like a blaring alarm or a tangible reason where I'd have to look in the mirror and say, "Okay, you have to stop this." But because I look exactly the same, it's like the evidence just completely vanishes by morning. My wife doesn't notice anything different about how I look, my doctor hasn't said anything about my BMI... it's just me and the empty wrappers in the trash can. So, no, to answer your question, no real weight gain at all, which I know sounds completely impossible given what I just told you, but it's the truth.
Do you feel guilty or ashamed while you are eating during these late-night episodes, or does that feeling come afterwards?

During it? No, during it, like I said, I'm just... I'm a passenger. I'm numb, almost. My brain is screaming, but I'm disconnected from it. But the second I stop... the absolute second I take that last bite and realize there's nothing left, or I finally just can't swallow another mouthful... that's when it hits me. It's like a ton of bricks. 

Afterward, I just... I feel so incredibly sick with myself. Physically sick from the food, sure, but mostly just... mentally, emotionally sick. I'll be standing there looking at the mess I made, you know, the empty cracker sleeves and the dirty forks and the cold Chinese food carton left out on the counter, and the shame is just overwhelming. It washes over me so fast. 

I mean, I'm a thirty-nine-year-old man. People... people look at me, my friends, my wife, my old colleagues from the office before I left... they see this guy who is supposed to be organized, right? Someone who is strong, someone who has his life together, pays the mortgage on time, keeps the yard looking nice, manages his responsibilities. That's the image I've built. That's who George is supposed to be. But then the reality is, I'm just sitting there in the dark kitchen, surrounded by crumbs, feeling absolutely ashamed and guilty and just... completely disgusted with myself. 

It's this heavy, sinking feeling in my chest. I'll be washing the fork so my wife doesn't find it in the sink the next morning, trying to bury the evidence deep in the trash can so she doesn't see how much I ate, and I just keep thinking, "How did you let this happen again? How are you this weak?" I literally just stand there hating myself for letting it happen again, for breaking the promise I made to myself just a few hours earlier when I swore I wouldn't do it. So yeah, the guilt... it's all afterward. And it's paralyzing, it really is. I just sit there in the quiet and just... I just feel totally disgusted that I'm this person now.
Do you feel like you are in control of your actions when you start eating at night?

Control? No. God, no. That is probably the scariest part of this whole thing, to be completely honest with you. If I had control, I wouldn't be doing this, right? I try so hard during the day. I tell myself all afternoon that tonight is going to be different, that I am just going to go to sleep like a normal person. But then... I don't know, it is like a switch flips. I walk into the kitchen, maybe just to get a glass of water, and I see something, or I open the fridge just to peek. And the second, the absolute millisecond I take that first bite... it is just over. 

It really feels like the decision has already been made for me. It is like I am watching myself from the outside. I will literally be standing there in my own kitchen, in the dark, and my brain is screaming at me. I am telling myself, George, stop now, you do not need this, put it down. But it is like my hands are not even listening to my brain. My hands just keep moving on their own. They keep fixing another plate, or reaching back into the fridge, or opening another container of leftovers, peeling back the plastic wrap, whatever it is. It is so mechanical. I will be watching my own hands tear open a bag or scoop out another massive portion, and my mind is just begging me to stop, but I cannot. 

It is like the physical part of me has completely hijacked the mental part. I have never experienced anything like it in any other area of my life. I mean, I used to manage things, I used to be in charge of my daily schedule and handle real responsibilities before I left my job in October, I know how to be in control of my actions. But when I am standing at that counter at two in the morning? I have absolutely zero control. None whatsoever. Once I take that first bite, my hands just take over and I am completely powerless to stop them from opening the next thing.
Are you aware of what you are eating and the amount of food you are consuming while you are eating during these late-night episodes?

Am I aware? I mean... yes and no. It’s complicated. Because, like I was just saying about watching my hands move, on some level, I know I’m opening the third sleeve of crackers or pulling out the second Tupperware container of leftover pasta. I see it happening. But the actual experience of eating it? The awareness of the sheer volume while it's actually going down? That is completely distorted. 

See, the thing is, I eat so fast during those times... it’s honestly like a race against my own brain. I eat so incredibly fast that I barely even taste the food. And that’s... that’s really sad for me, honestly, because I used to take so much pride in my cooking. Back before October, when my life had structure, I was the one making dinner for us. I’d spend an hour in the evening chopping fresh garlic, getting the seasoning just right, making sure the meat was perfectly seared. I loved the process, I loved the flavors. But at 2 AM? There is absolutely zero savoring. 

I’m literally just standing there at the kitchen counter—barefoot on the cold tile, not even bothering to turn on the overhead light or sit down at the table like a civilized person—and I am just shoveling it in. It's frantic. I’ll be swallowing these massive, big bites before I’ve even finished chewing the last one. It’s just... shove it in, barely chew, swallow, reach for more, repeat. It’s this desperate, panicked pace, like someone is about to come in and snatch the food away from me. 

So, to answer if I’m aware of the amount... by the time I actually stop, when the frenzy finally breaks and I look down at the empty containers, I’m always completely shocked. Because when you’re eating that quickly, when you’re just gulping down half-chewed food as fast as humanly possible without even tasting it, your brain doesn't register that you just consumed enough for three people in the span of ten minutes. You just don't feel it happening until it's over and you're left staring at the mess.
Do you feel any specific emotions right before you start eating at night, like anxiety or sadness?

Anxiety or sadness? You know... it's funny you ask that, because I've thought about that a lot. I think people assume—and honestly, I used to assume this too—that if you're doing something like this, you must be, I don't know, sitting in the dark sobbing into a bowl of ice cream or having a massive panic attack about your life. Especially since I've been out of the workforce since October, you'd think I'd be pacing the floors, wringing my hands with anxiety about the future or feeling deeply depressed right before I eat. But honestly? No. I don't feel anything like that right before it happens. 

If anything, it's the exact opposite of an emotion. It's... a void. A complete blankness. I'll just be sitting on the couch in the living room. My wife usually heads up to bed around 10:30 or 11:00, and I stay downstairs because my schedule is just completely wrecked these days. So it's quiet. The house is totally silent except for whatever I have on the TV, usually just some meaningless rerun or a history documentary turned down low so I don't wake her. I'm not feeling sad in those moments. I'm not feeling anxious. I'm not really feeling much of anything at all. 

It’s just this... this creeping sensation. Not an emotion, but a pull. It starts like a whisper in the back of my mind, just reminding me the kitchen is there. The leftovers are there. The pantry is there. And it gets louder and louder until it's the only thing I can focus on. But it’s not driven by a feeling, it's just... gravity. It just pulls me off the couch and into the kitchen. I honestly wish I could say I was triggered by a sudden wave of anxiety, because then maybe I could pinpoint it, you know? Maybe I could try some breathing exercises or tell myself to calm down. But no, there's no sadness or anxiety right before I start. It's just this numb, inevitable pull toward the food.
Have you ever been on a diet or restricted your food intake in any way before these late-night eating episodes started?

Dieting? No. No, not at all. I mean... I know that’s a huge thing for a lot of people, and it seems like everyone is always on some kind of keto or intermittent fasting kick these days, but I never really did any of that. 

Before all this started, I never really had to think about restricting my food, to be completely honest with you. Like I was saying earlier about how much I loved to cook—I would make these big, hearty, rich meals for us. I’m talking heavy cream sauces, big cuts of meat, homemade breads, you name it. I never once looked at a plate of food and thought about calories or macros or whatever it is people track on their phones. I just ate what tasted good, and I ate until I was full, and that was that. I never felt the need to hold back or deprive myself. 

It’s actually kind of ironic, because my wife, she’ll sometimes try to cut back on carbs, you know, if we have a vacation coming up or a wedding to go to or something, and she’ll be eating salads while I’m sitting there putting away a massive plate of lasagna. And I never gained a pound doing it. I guess when I was still working, before October, my schedule just kept me active enough, or my metabolism was just handling it. I never had this... this adversarial relationship with food where I felt like I had to put a padlock on what I was allowed to eat during the day. 

So, no, I wasn't starving myself or trying some strict diet right before these late-night episodes kicked off. Food was just... food. It was just a normal, enjoyable part of my day. It was something I looked forward to preparing and sharing. I never restricted anything. That’s part of why this whole thing is so incredibly baffling to me. It’s not like I’m sitting around all day denying myself a piece of bread and then snapping at midnight because I’m starving. I just... I never had rules about food before. It was never something I had to control, until suddenly it was the only thing controlling me.
Have you experienced any significant life changes or particularly stressful events around the time these late-night eating episodes started?

Significant life changes? Yeah... yeah, you could definitely say that. 

I know I mentioned earlier that I've been out of the workforce since October, and obviously, that was a massive blow, but the truth is, the wheels started coming off long before that. The job loss was just kind of the final nail in the coffin. The real nightmare, the thing that actually kicked all of this off, is our house. We... well, we're losing it. The bank is taking it. 

It started with just falling behind on a couple of mortgage payments. You know how it is, or maybe you don't, but you think you can catch up. You shuffle some money around, you ignore a few phone calls from unknown numbers, you tell yourself it’s just a temporary rough patch and you'll figure it out next month. But then the letters start coming. Those thick, certified envelopes from the bank. I remember every time the mail carrier came up the driveway, my stomach would just drop right out of me. I’d actually wait by the window and intercept the mail so my wife wouldn't have to see it right away, just to buy us a few more hours of peace before we had to have another awful conversation about money. 

The actual foreclosure process... that officially started about a year and two months now. And honestly, looking back on it, that’s exactly when all of this late-night eating began. It’s been going on since the foreclosure process started, about a year and two months now. It tracks perfectly. Because before that, like I said, I was cooking, we were happy, things felt secure. But once that first official legal notice arrived, once it became a real, terrifying legal process and not just a missed payment... something in me just snapped. 

I felt—and still feel—like such an absolute failure. As a husband, as a man, as a provider. It’s this constant, suffocating pressure hanging over our heads every single day, just not knowing when the sheriff is going to show up and tape a notice to our front door telling us we have to vacate. So, yeah, it’s been a year and two months of living in absolute limbo. A year and two months of me standing in that dark kitchen at 2 AM, trying to numb out the fact that the roof over my head isn't even really mine anymore. So if you're looking for a stressful event to tie all this to, that's definitely the one. That's the anchor for this whole mess.
Have you ever tried to stop or cut back on these late-night eating episodes?

Tried to stop? Oh, God, yes. Every single day. I wake up in the morning, usually feeling completely miserable and full of regret, and I tell myself, tonight is the night we don't do this. I'll even sit on the couch in the evening and mentally rehearse it. I'll think, okay, when she goes upstairs, I'm just going to drink a glass of water, turn off the TV, and go straight to sleep. I'll try to set all these little mental traps for myself, you know? Like leaving the kitchen light off so I won't want to go in there, or telling myself I'll just read a book instead—even though my focus is completely shot these days with everything going on with the bank. 

But despite all those promises I make to myself during the day... it's like I have two entirely different brains. There's the logical brain that desperately wants to stop, that knows how much worse I'm going to feel, and then there's this other part of me that just completely hijacks the system the second I cross the threshold into the kitchen. 

And the terrifying part, the part that really makes me feel like I'm losing my mind, is that once I take that first bite—just one single bite of a leftover or a piece of cheese or whatever is sitting in the fridge—it feels like the decision has already been made for me. It's like a switch flips in my head and the brakes are just gone. And the craziest thing is that I am fully aware of it happening. I'm not in a trance. I'll literally be standing there at the counter, chewing, and my inner voice is just pleading with me. I'm in my own head telling myself, "George, stop now. Put it down, George. Just walk away." 

But it's like my body is completely disconnected from my brain. Even while I’m telling myself to stop, my hands just keep going. My hands keep fixing another plate or opening another container, peeling back the foil on a casserole dish, tearing into another bag from the pantry. It’s like I’m a passenger in my own body, just standing behind my own eyes watching myself do this, completely unable to stop the momentum. I try so hard to pull back, I really do, but that total loss of control... it just overrides everything I want. It’s exhausting. It is just so utterly exhausting to fight yourself like that and lose every single time.
Have you ever talked to a doctor or a therapist about your late-night eating episodes before?

Talked to a doctor? Or a therapist? No. No, absolutely not. You are actually the very first person I am sitting down with to discuss any of this. 

I mean, I used to go to my regular physician for, you know, the standard yearly check-ups—at least I did before the job loss in October messed up my insurance situation. But even when I was going, I’d just sit there on that crinkly paper on the exam table and we’d talk about my blood pressure or my cholesterol, which were always perfectly fine, by the way. I never once brought up the eating. I mean, how do you even broach a subject like that? How do you look a medical professional in the eye and say, "Hey Doc, by the way, I spend my nights standing in the dark gorging myself on cold leftovers until my stomach physically hurts"? The shame of it... it’s just so incredibly heavy. I couldn't bring myself to say the words out loud.

And as for a therapist... no, I’ve never seen one. I know therapy is supposed to be great, and I know it helps a lot of people, but I guess I just always grew up with this mindset that you handle your own problems. You know? You’re a man, you pull yourself up by your bootstraps, you figure it out, you power through. Especially with everything going on with the house and the bank... I felt like I had to be the rock for my wife. If I admitted that I was crumbling, if I went to a shrink because I couldn't even control what I was putting in my mouth in the middle of the night... I don't know, it just felt like admitting total, absolute defeat. Like I was completely broken. 

So, I kept it entirely to myself. I haven’t even told my wife the full extent of what goes on downstairs while she’s asleep. She knows I snack, but she doesn't know *this*. It’s just been this massive, suffocating secret that I’ve been carrying around entirely on my own for the past year and two months. So, yeah, no doctors, no therapists. Just me, trying to fix it myself, and failing every single time, until I finally ended up here.

patient.answer:
Well, hi. Thanks for seeing me. I, uh, I guess I'm here because things have just gotten really out of hand lately. You see, I'm not working right now, so I'm around the house all day, but it's really the nights that are the main problem for me. Most nights, after my wife goes up to bed—she usually heads up around 10 or 10:30 because she likes to read a bit before sleep, and the house just gets so incredibly quiet—I almost always end up wandering into the kitchen. 

And it's not like I'm just grabbing a normal midnight snack, you know, like a piece of fruit or a cracker. I start eating, and I eat way, way past what anyone would ever consider a normal plate of food. Like, if we had a family get-together or a party recently, I'll pull out all the heavy stuff. The cold fried chicken, the big Tupperware containers of mac and cheese, the sweet potatoes, those little dinner rolls... really just whatever event leftovers are sitting in there. I'll tell myself I'm just having a taste, but then I'm having another, and another, and I just keep going and going until an entire catering tray is completely scraped clean, or literally half the food in the fridge is just... gone. I don't even know how I fit it all in sometimes, but I'll just stand there in the kitchen and completely clear out whatever we have stored away. It's just happening almost every single night now, and I just... I don't know, it's a lot.

inference.note: Added F50.8 and F50.9 as initial candidates due to the patient's description of binge eating behaviors at night.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences guilt or shame after binge eating
doctor.question: How do you feel after one of these late-night eating episodes?

Well, honestly... it's just awful. I mean, physically I feel terrible, obviously, because I've just stuffed myself to the brim, but mentally... mentally it's just this crushing weight. Like, immediately after I finish that last bite, or when I look down and see the empty containers stacked up on the counter, it just hits me all at once. I feel so incredibly sick with myself. 

And it's not just a passing thought, you know? It's this deep, heavy feeling in my gut. I think about how people see me—my wife, my friends, the people I used to work with. They all think of me as this organized, capable, strong guy who has everything under control. But then there I am, standing in the kitchen in the middle of the night, surrounded by crumbs and empty Tupperware, and I just feel so ashamed. I feel guilty for wasting the food, guilty for hiding it from my wife, and just absolutely disgusted with myself that I let it happen again. I always tell myself, "Okay, tonight's the night I stop, tonight I'll just have a glass of water and go back to bed," but then I don't. And when it's over, the disgust is just... it's overwhelming. I just sit there in the quiet and think, "What is wrong with me?" It's like I'm two different people, the guy during the day and this... this person at night who just completely loses control.

No, no, I've never done anything like that. I know some people do, you know, they throw up or take pills to try and undo it, but I just... I don't. I just sit there with it. I mean, the thought of making myself sick, it just doesn't even cross my mind, really. I just feel so heavy, physically and emotionally, and I just kind of drag myself back up the stairs to bed. 

It's actually kind of funny, in a dark way, because I'll lie there in the dark, and my stomach will be in absolute knots, just stretching and aching from all that food—like that time last week after my niece's birthday party, I ate maybe three-quarters of a sheet cake all by myself, plus I don't even know how many leftover hot dogs, and I was just lying there sweating, feeling like I was going to burst. But I just ride it out. I just lie there and let the guilt and the stomachache just wash over me until I finally manage to pass out. I don't try to get rid of it. I just... I just carry it. Literally and figuratively, I guess. I just wake up the next morning feeling bloated and gross and exhausted, and the cycle just starts all over again. But no, no throwing up, no laxatives, nothing like that. I just suffer through the aftermath.

inference.note: F50.9 was ruled out as the patient does not use compensatory behaviors such as self-induced vomiting or misuse of laxatives, which is more characteristic of bulimia nervosa, whereas the described behavior aligns more closely with binge eating disorder.

doctor.intent: determine frequency of binge eating episodes

patient.answer:
Well, it's... it's a lot. I mean, if I really sit back and think about it, it's been going on for months now. Honestly, for months, I can't think of a single week where it didn't happen at least once. Not one week. And, you know, it's rarely just once. Most weeks, it's several nights. 

Like I was saying before, it's always after my wife goes up to bed. She's got her routine, right? Brushes her teeth, washes her face, gets into bed with her book—lately she's been reading these thick historical biographies, so she's up there for a good while before she actually turns the light out. And I'll just be downstairs. I might be watching TV, or scrolling on my phone, or just sitting there in the living room, and the house gets so quiet you can hear the hum of the refrigerator. And that's when it starts. 

So, yeah, it's several nights a week. Sometimes it's three nights, sometimes it's four or five. Last week, I think it was Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. It's just this constant, looming thing. I'll wake up in the morning and tell myself, "Okay, tonight is going to be different. Tonight I'm just going to watch the game, drink some water, and go to sleep." But then 10:30 rolls around, she heads upstairs, and it's like a switch flips in my brain. The pull to go into the kitchen is just so strong. I'll walk in there, open the fridge, and it's like I'm on autopilot. Before I know it, it's happened again. So, to answer your question, it's almost constantly happening. Multiple times a week, every single week, for months on end now. I just can't seem to break the cycle.

doctor.question: Do you notice any specific emotions or thoughts that trigger your desire to eat at night?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about specific emotional or cognitive triggers that precede the binge-eating episodes. The symptom profile does not contain an item specifically addressing triggers or emotional states prior to eating.

patient.answer:
Well, that's... that's the thing, I'm not really sure. I mean, I've tried to sit down and figure it out, you know? Like, really analyze what's going through my head right before I start eating. I'll sit there in the living room, and I'll try to pinpoint, "Okay, am I sad right now? Am I stressed about money? Am I worried about finding a job?" Because, you know, being out of work right now, there's a lot of stress. I left my last job back in October, and it's been this constant weight. So you'd think it would be that, right? You'd think I'd be sitting there worrying about the mortgage or whatever, and then I'd go eat to feel better.

But honestly... I don't really notice anything specific like that. It's not like I'm sitting there crying or having a panic attack and then I run to the fridge. It's more just... this emptiness, almost? Or maybe just boredom? I don't know if boredom is the right word, because it feels more intense than just being bored. But it's just this quiet. The house is so quiet. My wife is upstairs, the dog is asleep on his bed in the corner, the TV is just kind of murmuring in the background, and there's just... nothing happening. And it's almost like the quiet itself is the trigger. 

I don't have this big, flashing thought of, "I am so upset, I need a sandwich." It's more like a physical pull. I just start thinking about the kitchen. I'll picture the leftover lasagna in the Tupperware with the red lid, or the bag of chips sitting on the second shelf of the pantry, right next to the peanut butter. And once that image is in my head, it's just... it's all I can think about. But as for an actual emotion or a specific worry? I really haven't noticed one. It just feels like an automatic response to the house being empty and quiet, like my brain just says, "Well, it's time to go eat now," and I just get up and do it without really feeling anything at all until the guilt hits me afterward.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient has a lack of control during the eating episodes
doctor.question: Do you feel like you have control over what you're eating or the amount you're eating during these late-night episodes?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I take that first bite, it feels like the decision has already been made for me, and even while I’m telling myself, 'George, stop now,' my hands keep fixing another plate or opening another container.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about feeling a lack of control over what or how much is being eaten during the episodes, which matches the Loss of Control symptom.

patient.answer:
No. No, none at all. That's the scariest part, honestly. It's like... it's like I'm not even driving the car anymore. I'm just in the passenger seat watching it crash. 

I'll be standing there in the kitchen, right? The refrigerator door is open, the little light is on, casting that weird glow on the linoleum, and I'll tell myself, "Okay, George, just one slice of cheese. Just one slice and we go back to the couch." But then I take that first bite, and it's like... it's like the decision has already been made for me. The cheese is gone, and then I'm reaching for the leftover Chinese food in the back, the one in the white carton with the metal handle, and I'm not even heating it up. I'm just eating cold lo mein straight out of the box with a fork I grabbed from the drying rack. 

And the whole time, my brain is screaming at me. I'm literally standing there, chewing, and I'm telling myself, "George, stop now. Put the fork down. Close the carton. Put it back." I'm having this entire internal argument with myself, begging myself to stop, but my hands... my hands just keep moving. They keep fixing another plate, or opening another container, or tearing open a bag of pretzels. It's like my body has been hijacked. I'll finish the Chinese food, and then I'll move on to a sleeve of crackers, and then maybe a bowl of cereal, pouring the milk in so carefully so it doesn't splash and make a sound that might wake my wife up. 

I know I'm full. I know I shouldn't be eating it. I know how awful I'm going to feel in twenty minutes, but I just can't physically make myself stop until I'm so stuffed I can barely breathe. It's completely out of my hands once I start. Completely.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's late-night eating episodes are related to a lack of hunger before starting to eat
doctor.question: Do you usually feel hungry before you start eating at night?

target_item.name: Eating_Without_Hunger
target_item.manifestation: A lot of the time I’m not hungry at all—I may have just eaten dinner with my wife—but later I still go back and start picking at leftovers until it turns into another full-on spread.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel physically hungry before the late-night eating episodes, which corresponds directly to the symptom of eating without hunger.

patient.answer:
No, not really. Actually, a lot of the time I'm not hungry at all. I mean, it's crazy when you think about it, because you'd assume someone eating that much food must be starving, right? Like they haven't eaten a single thing all day. But for me, it's... it's the exact opposite. 

I might have just eaten a really big, filling dinner with my wife. Like, just a few days ago, she made this huge shepherd's pie—she uses ground turkey instead of beef to be a little healthier, and puts this nice thick crust of mashed potatoes on top with a little paprika—and we sat down at the dining table, ate a proper meal together, had a side salad with it, the whole nine yards. I was full. I was completely, totally satisfied. My stomach was physically full. 

But then, you know, a couple of hours pass, she goes upstairs to read her book like I mentioned before, and even though my stomach is literally still digesting dinner, even though there is absolutely zero physical hunger... I still go back into the kitchen. I'll just start picking at the leftovers. I'll take a fork and just kind of shave off a little piece of the pie from the pan on the stove while I'm supposed to be putting it away in the Tupperware. And then maybe I take a little more. And then I'm pulling out other things from the fridge, maybe some cheese, maybe some bread, and before I know it, it turns into another full-on spread right there on the counter. 

It's not about hunger at all. My stomach isn't growling. I'm not feeling weak or lightheaded or anything that tells your body it's time to eat. I just start picking at things, and then it snowballs into this massive amount of food, even though I'm already completely full from the dinner I just had. So, yeah, hunger really doesn't have anything to do with it. It's just... it's something else entirely, and I don't really know how to stop it once I start picking.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient has experienced significant weight gain due to the eating episodes
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant weight gain since these late-night eating episodes started?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about weight gain, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
You know, that's the one thing that really confuses me about all of this. Because you would think, with the sheer volume of food I'm putting away—like I said, the whole cartons of Chinese food, the sleeves of crackers, the blocks of cheese—you'd think I'd be putting on ten pounds a week, right? I mean, it's just basic math, calories in versus calories out. But... no. I actually haven't noticed any major weight gain at all. 

It's the strangest thing. I still step on the scale in our master bathroom—it's this older digital one we got at Target years ago, the kind where you have to tap it with your foot first to wake it up before you actually step on it—and the number really hasn't budged much. Maybe a pound or two fluctuating, which I think is pretty normal for anyone, depending on water weight or whatever. And my clothes still fit exactly the same. I have these khaki pants I used to wear to the office before I left in October, and I put them on the other day just to see. Just out of pure paranoia, really, because I was sitting there thinking, "George, there's no way you aren't ballooning up with all this garbage you're eating at 2 AM." But they buttoned up just fine. No pinching at the waist, no having to suck in my gut to get the zipper up. 

It's almost like my body is just... I don't know, ignoring it? Or maybe my metabolism is just naturally fast enough to handle it right now? I really don't know how it's physically possible, but it almost makes me feel worse in a way. Because it's like this invisible secret. If I were gaining a ton of weight, at least there would be a physical sign of what I'm doing to myself, right? Like a blaring alarm or a tangible reason where I'd have to look in the mirror and say, "Okay, you have to stop this." But because I look exactly the same, it's like the evidence just completely vanishes by morning. My wife doesn't notice anything different about how I look, my doctor hasn't said anything about my BMI... it's just me and the empty wrappers in the trash can. So, no, to answer your question, no real weight gain at all, which I know sounds completely impossible given what I just told you, but it's the truth.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences guilt or shame specifically related to the act of eating itself, rather than just the consequences of eating

target_item.name: Negative_Affect_After_Binge

patient.answer:
During it? No, during it, like I said, I'm just... I'm a passenger. I'm numb, almost. My brain is screaming, but I'm disconnected from it. But the second I stop... the absolute second I take that last bite and realize there's nothing left, or I finally just can't swallow another mouthful... that's when it hits me. It's like a ton of bricks. 

Afterward, I just... I feel so incredibly sick with myself. Physically sick from the food, sure, but mostly just... mentally, emotionally sick. I'll be standing there looking at the mess I made, you know, the empty cracker sleeves and the dirty forks and the cold Chinese food carton left out on the counter, and the shame is just overwhelming. It washes over me so fast. 

I mean, I'm a thirty-nine-year-old man. People... people look at me, my friends, my wife, my old colleagues from the office before I left... they see this guy who is supposed to be organized, right? Someone who is strong, someone who has his life together, pays the mortgage on time, keeps the yard looking nice, manages his responsibilities. That's the image I've built. That's who George is supposed to be. But then the reality is, I'm just sitting there in the dark kitchen, surrounded by crumbs, feeling absolutely ashamed and guilty and just... completely disgusted with myself. 

It's this heavy, sinking feeling in my chest. I'll be washing the fork so my wife doesn't find it in the sink the next morning, trying to bury the evidence deep in the trash can so she doesn't see how much I ate, and I just keep thinking, "How did you let this happen again? How are you this weak?" I literally just stand there hating myself for letting it happen again, for breaking the promise I made to myself just a few hours earlier when I swore I wouldn't do it. So yeah, the guilt... it's all afterward. And it's paralyzing, it really is. I just sit there in the quiet and just... I just feel totally disgusted that I'm this person now.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences loss of control during the binge-eating episodes
doctor.question: Do you feel like you are in control of your actions when you start eating at night?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I take that first bite, it feels like the decision has already been made for me, and even while I’m telling myself, 'George, stop now,' my hands keep fixing another plate or opening another container.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if I feel in control of my actions when I start eating at night, which corresponds to the 'Loss of Control' symptom.

patient.answer:
Control? No. God, no. That is probably the scariest part of this whole thing, to be completely honest with you. If I had control, I wouldn't be doing this, right? I try so hard during the day. I tell myself all afternoon that tonight is going to be different, that I am just going to go to sleep like a normal person. But then... I don't know, it is like a switch flips. I walk into the kitchen, maybe just to get a glass of water, and I see something, or I open the fridge just to peek. And the second, the absolute millisecond I take that first bite... it is just over. 

It really feels like the decision has already been made for me. It is like I am watching myself from the outside. I will literally be standing there in my own kitchen, in the dark, and my brain is screaming at me. I am telling myself, George, stop now, you do not need this, put it down. But it is like my hands are not even listening to my brain. My hands just keep moving on their own. They keep fixing another plate, or reaching back into the fridge, or opening another container of leftovers, peeling back the plastic wrap, whatever it is. It is so mechanical. I will be watching my own hands tear open a bag or scoop out another massive portion, and my mind is just begging me to stop, but I cannot. 

It is like the physical part of me has completely hijacked the mental part. I have never experienced anything like it in any other area of my life. I mean, I used to manage things, I used to be in charge of my daily schedule and handle real responsibilities before I left my job in October, I know how to be in control of my actions. But when I am standing at that counter at two in the morning? I have absolutely zero control. None whatsoever. Once I take that first bite, my hands just take over and I am completely powerless to stop them from opening the next thing.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient has any awareness of their eating behavior during the episodes
doctor.question: Are you aware of what you are eating and the amount of food you are consuming while you are eating during these late-night episodes?

target_item.name: Rapid_Eating

patient.answer:
Am I aware? I mean... yes and no. It’s complicated. Because, like I was just saying about watching my hands move, on some level, I know I’m opening the third sleeve of crackers or pulling out the second Tupperware container of leftover pasta. I see it happening. But the actual experience of eating it? The awareness of the sheer volume while it's actually going down? That is completely distorted. 

See, the thing is, I eat so fast during those times... it’s honestly like a race against my own brain. I eat so incredibly fast that I barely even taste the food. And that’s... that’s really sad for me, honestly, because I used to take so much pride in my cooking. Back before October, when my life had structure, I was the one making dinner for us. I’d spend an hour in the evening chopping fresh garlic, getting the seasoning just right, making sure the meat was perfectly seared. I loved the process, I loved the flavors. But at 2 AM? There is absolutely zero savoring. 

I’m literally just standing there at the kitchen counter—barefoot on the cold tile, not even bothering to turn on the overhead light or sit down at the table like a civilized person—and I am just shoveling it in. It's frantic. I’ll be swallowing these massive, big bites before I’ve even finished chewing the last one. It’s just... shove it in, barely chew, swallow, reach for more, repeat. It’s this desperate, panicked pace, like someone is about to come in and snatch the food away from me. 

So, to answer if I’m aware of the amount... by the time I actually stop, when the frenzy finally breaks and I look down at the empty containers, I’m always completely shocked. Because when you’re eating that quickly, when you’re just gulping down half-chewed food as fast as humanly possible without even tasting it, your brain doesn't register that you just consumed enough for three people in the span of ten minutes. You just don't feel it happening until it's over and you're left staring at the mess.

doctor.intent: understand if patient experiences any emotional triggers before the late-night eating episodes
doctor.question: Do you feel any specific emotions right before you start eating at night, like anxiety or sadness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotions or triggers right before the binge eating episode begins. The symptom profile covers negative affect after the binge (S055), but does not contain an item for emotions experienced prior to the binge.

patient.answer:
Anxiety or sadness? You know... it's funny you ask that, because I've thought about that a lot. I think people assume—and honestly, I used to assume this too—that if you're doing something like this, you must be, I don't know, sitting in the dark sobbing into a bowl of ice cream or having a massive panic attack about your life. Especially since I've been out of the workforce since October, you'd think I'd be pacing the floors, wringing my hands with anxiety about the future or feeling deeply depressed right before I eat. But honestly? No. I don't feel anything like that right before it happens. 

If anything, it's the exact opposite of an emotion. It's... a void. A complete blankness. I'll just be sitting on the couch in the living room. My wife usually heads up to bed around 10:30 or 11:00, and I stay downstairs because my schedule is just completely wrecked these days. So it's quiet. The house is totally silent except for whatever I have on the TV, usually just some meaningless rerun or a history documentary turned down low so I don't wake her. I'm not feeling sad in those moments. I'm not feeling anxious. I'm not really feeling much of anything at all. 

It’s just this... this creeping sensation. Not an emotion, but a pull. It starts like a whisper in the back of my mind, just reminding me the kitchen is there. The leftovers are there. The pantry is there. And it gets louder and louder until it's the only thing I can focus on. But it’s not driven by a feeling, it's just... gravity. It just pulls me off the couch and into the kitchen. I honestly wish I could say I was triggered by a sudden wave of anxiety, because then maybe I could pinpoint it, you know? Maybe I could try some breathing exercises or tell myself to calm down. But no, there's no sadness or anxiety right before I start. It's just this numb, inevitable pull toward the food.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has any history of dieting or restrictive eating patterns
doctor.question: Have you ever been on a diet or restricted your food intake in any way before these late-night eating episodes started?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of dieting or food restriction, which is not covered by any of the specific symptom profiles provided.

patient.answer:
Dieting? No. No, not at all. I mean... I know that’s a huge thing for a lot of people, and it seems like everyone is always on some kind of keto or intermittent fasting kick these days, but I never really did any of that. 

Before all this started, I never really had to think about restricting my food, to be completely honest with you. Like I was saying earlier about how much I loved to cook—I would make these big, hearty, rich meals for us. I’m talking heavy cream sauces, big cuts of meat, homemade breads, you name it. I never once looked at a plate of food and thought about calories or macros or whatever it is people track on their phones. I just ate what tasted good, and I ate until I was full, and that was that. I never felt the need to hold back or deprive myself. 

It’s actually kind of ironic, because my wife, she’ll sometimes try to cut back on carbs, you know, if we have a vacation coming up or a wedding to go to or something, and she’ll be eating salads while I’m sitting there putting away a massive plate of lasagna. And I never gained a pound doing it. I guess when I was still working, before October, my schedule just kept me active enough, or my metabolism was just handling it. I never had this... this adversarial relationship with food where I felt like I had to put a padlock on what I was allowed to eat during the day. 

So, no, I wasn't starving myself or trying some strict diet right before these late-night episodes kicked off. Food was just... food. It was just a normal, enjoyable part of my day. It was something I looked forward to preparing and sharing. I never restricted anything. That’s part of why this whole thing is so incredibly baffling to me. It’s not like I’m sitting around all day denying myself a piece of bread and then snapping at midnight because I’m starving. I just... I never had rules about food before. It was never something I had to control, until suddenly it was the only thing controlling me.

doctor.intent: determine if patient has experienced any stressors or significant life changes
doctor.question: Have you experienced any significant life changes or particularly stressful events around the time these late-night eating episodes started?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since the foreclosure process started, about a year and two months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about stressful life events around the time the episodes began, which matches the patient's onset of symptoms corresponding to the start of the foreclosure process.

patient.answer:
Significant life changes? Yeah... yeah, you could definitely say that. 

I know I mentioned earlier that I've been out of the workforce since October, and obviously, that was a massive blow, but the truth is, the wheels started coming off long before that. The job loss was just kind of the final nail in the coffin. The real nightmare, the thing that actually kicked all of this off, is our house. We... well, we're losing it. The bank is taking it. 

It started with just falling behind on a couple of mortgage payments. You know how it is, or maybe you don't, but you think you can catch up. You shuffle some money around, you ignore a few phone calls from unknown numbers, you tell yourself it’s just a temporary rough patch and you'll figure it out next month. But then the letters start coming. Those thick, certified envelopes from the bank. I remember every time the mail carrier came up the driveway, my stomach would just drop right out of me. I’d actually wait by the window and intercept the mail so my wife wouldn't have to see it right away, just to buy us a few more hours of peace before we had to have another awful conversation about money. 

The actual foreclosure process... that officially started about a year and two months now. And honestly, looking back on it, that’s exactly when all of this late-night eating began. It’s been going on since the foreclosure process started, about a year and two months now. It tracks perfectly. Because before that, like I said, I was cooking, we were happy, things felt secure. But once that first official legal notice arrived, once it became a real, terrifying legal process and not just a missed payment... something in me just snapped. 

I felt—and still feel—like such an absolute failure. As a husband, as a man, as a provider. It’s this constant, suffocating pressure hanging over our heads every single day, just not knowing when the sheriff is going to show up and tape a notice to our front door telling us we have to vacate. So, yeah, it’s been a year and two months of living in absolute limbo. A year and two months of me standing in that dark kitchen at 2 AM, trying to numb out the fact that the roof over my head isn't even really mine anymore. So if you're looking for a stressful event to tie all this to, that's definitely the one. That's the anchor for this whole mess.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has tried to stop or control the late-night eating episodes

patient.answer:
Tried to stop? Oh, God, yes. Every single day. I wake up in the morning, usually feeling completely miserable and full of regret, and I tell myself, tonight is the night we don't do this. I'll even sit on the couch in the evening and mentally rehearse it. I'll think, okay, when she goes upstairs, I'm just going to drink a glass of water, turn off the TV, and go straight to sleep. I'll try to set all these little mental traps for myself, you know? Like leaving the kitchen light off so I won't want to go in there, or telling myself I'll just read a book instead—even though my focus is completely shot these days with everything going on with the bank. 

But despite all those promises I make to myself during the day... it's like I have two entirely different brains. There's the logical brain that desperately wants to stop, that knows how much worse I'm going to feel, and then there's this other part of me that just completely hijacks the system the second I cross the threshold into the kitchen. 

And the terrifying part, the part that really makes me feel like I'm losing my mind, is that once I take that first bite—just one single bite of a leftover or a piece of cheese or whatever is sitting in the fridge—it feels like the decision has already been made for me. It's like a switch flips in my head and the brakes are just gone. And the craziest thing is that I am fully aware of it happening. I'm not in a trance. I'll literally be standing there at the counter, chewing, and my inner voice is just pleading with me. I'm in my own head telling myself, "George, stop now. Put it down, George. Just walk away." 

But it's like my body is completely disconnected from my brain. Even while I’m telling myself to stop, my hands just keep going. My hands keep fixing another plate or opening another container, peeling back the foil on a casserole dish, tearing into another bag from the pantry. It’s like I’m a passenger in my own body, just standing behind my own eyes watching myself do this, completely unable to stop the momentum. I try so hard to pull back, I really do, but that total loss of control... it just overrides everything I want. It’s exhausting. It is just so utterly exhausting to fight yourself like that and lose every single time.

doctor.intent: determine if patient has attempted to seek help for their eating issue
doctor.question: Have you ever talked to a doctor or a therapist about your late-night eating episodes before?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about prior medical or psychiatric consultations for the eating episodes, which is not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Talked to a doctor? Or a therapist? No. No, absolutely not. You are actually the very first person I am sitting down with to discuss any of this. 

I mean, I used to go to my regular physician for, you know, the standard yearly check-ups—at least I did before the job loss in October messed up my insurance situation. But even when I was going, I’d just sit there on that crinkly paper on the exam table and we’d talk about my blood pressure or my cholesterol, which were always perfectly fine, by the way. I never once brought up the eating. I mean, how do you even broach a subject like that? How do you look a medical professional in the eye and say, "Hey Doc, by the way, I spend my nights standing in the dark gorging myself on cold leftovers until my stomach physically hurts"? The shame of it... it’s just so incredibly heavy. I couldn't bring myself to say the words out loud.

And as for a therapist... no, I’ve never seen one. I know therapy is supposed to be great, and I know it helps a lot of people, but I guess I just always grew up with this mindset that you handle your own problems. You know? You’re a man, you pull yourself up by your bootstraps, you figure it out, you power through. Especially with everything going on with the house and the bank... I felt like I had to be the rock for my wife. If I admitted that I was crumbling, if I went to a shrink because I couldn't even control what I was putting in my mouth in the middle of the night... I don't know, it just felt like admitting total, absolute defeat. Like I was completely broken. 

So, I kept it entirely to myself. I haven’t even told my wife the full extent of what goes on downstairs while she’s asleep. She knows I snack, but she doesn't know *this*. It’s just been this massive, suffocating secret that I’ve been carrying around entirely on my own for the past year and two months. So, yeah, no doctors, no therapists. Just me, trying to fix it myself, and failing every single time, until I finally ended up here.
